title: Rotated sorted array
sub: One half is always sorted: search, minimum and rotation point — and why duplicates take O(log n) away
cards/0/title: The problem and why plain search breaks
cards/0/body:
Search in Rotated Sorted Array (LeetCode #33). An array of distinct numbers was sorted in ascending order and then rotated at an unknown point: [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7] → [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]. Find the index of target or −1 in O(log n); n ≤ 5000.

The signals — “sorted” and “O(log n)” — say binary search. But the plain version breaks. In [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], searching for 0, the middle is 7; it is greater than zero, so plain search goes left, while the zero is on the right. The invariant “everything right of mid is greater” is false here, and comparing a[mid] with target no longer tells you the direction by itself.

The naive solution is a linear scan, O(n). It is correct and worth naming, but the problem explicitly asks for O(log n).

In a game a rotated array is a ring buffer — for example, a position history for lag-compensated hit checks: time keeps growing, but the data starts at the buffer head rather than at slot zero. If the head is known, the rotation is no obstacle: the index (head + k) % n turns the buffer into an ordinary sorted array. Problem #33 is the case where the head is unknown.
cards/1/q: nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], target = 0. What does the plain binary search from the previous lesson do?
cards/1/options/0: mid = 3, 7 > 0 → hi = 2; then it searches [4, 5, 6] and returns −1
cards/1/options/1: Finds 0 in three comparisons: the array is almost sorted
cards/1/explain: Plain search trusts the invariant “everything right of mid is greater than target”, but right of the 7 sit 0, 1, 2. It dutifully throws away the right half together with the answer and, not finding 0 in [4, 5, 6], returns −1. No runtime error — just a wrong answer, which is worse: a bug like this passes half the tests.
cards/1/wrong/1: “Almost sorted” does not help: on the very first step 7 > 0 sends the search into the left half, and the zero is on the right.
cards/1/wrong/2: mid always stays inside [lo..hi], and hi = mid − 1 does not leave the array: the search simply ends with −1.
cards/1/wrong/3: The interval shrinks on every step, just as in plain search — the loop ends, but with a wrong answer.
cards/2/body:
Cut [lo..hi] at mid into the halves [lo..mid] and [mid..hi]. A rotated array has exactly one place where the value drops (7 → 0) — the rotation point. It can land in at most one half, so the other one is sorted. Which one takes a single comparison: if a[lo] <= a[mid], there is no drop on the left and [lo..mid] is sorted; otherwise [mid..hi] is sorted.

In the sorted half you can check in O(1) whether target lies there — by its ends: for the left half, a[lo] <= target && target < a[mid]. If it does, go there. If not, target can only be in the other half, even though that one contains the drop. The invariant is the same as before: if target exists, it is in [lo..hi]. Each step discards half — O(log n).

Why <= and not <: with two candidates mid == lo, and the left “half” is the single element a[lo]. It is sorted, but a[lo] < a[mid] is false, so the code would decide the right half is sorted — and check target against the ends of a segment that contains the drop.
cards/2/flow/1: a[lo] ≤ a[mid] → left sorted: target in [a[lo], a[mid]) ? left : right
cards/2/flow/2: otherwise right sorted: target in (a[mid], a[hi]] ? right : left
cards/3/q: Build the search in a rotated array.
cards/3/explain: The left half is sorted if a[lo] <= a[mid] — with equality for the lo == mid case. In it target lies in [a[lo], a[mid]): a[mid] is already checked, hence strictly less. In the right half it is (a[mid], a[hi]], right end included. Target is in the right half — go there: lo = mid + 1.
cards/4/task: Search for 53 in [41, 53, 55, 57, 58, 7, 8, 13, 20, 33, 37]. The rig will stop twice and ask which half the code treats as sorted and where it goes next.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Left [41..55] is sorted, 53 is in it → hi = mid − 1
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Left [41..55] is sorted, 53 is not in it → lo = mid + 1
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Both halves are sorted — the code cannot decide and does lo++
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: The candidates are indices [0..4]: 41, 53, 55, 57, 58. mid = 2, a[mid] = 55. What does the code do?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: a[lo] = 41 ≤ 55 — no drop on the left, the left half is sorted. 41 ≤ 53 < 55 — target is inside, so the right part is discarded together with mid: hi = 1. That the right half [55..58] happens to be sorted too does not matter to the code: it checks the left half first, and if target is not there, it goes right.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: a[lo] <= a[mid] — left [41..41]; 53 is not in it → lo = 1
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: a[lo] <= a[mid] — left [41..41]; 53 is not in it → hi = −1
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: The else branch — right [41..53]; 53 is in it → lo = 1
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: The candidates are [0..1]: 41 and 53. mid = lo = 0, a[mid] = 41. Which branch does the code take, and where does it move?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: This is exactly the mid == lo case: the left “half” is the single element 41. The condition a[lo] <= a[mid] (41 <= 41) is true, 53 is not in [41, 41), so target is further right: lo = mid + 1 = 1. With < the code would take the else branch and here would happen to reach lo = 1 as well — but on another array it would go wrong.
cards/5/q: On nums = [3, 1] with target = 1 this code returns −1. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/5/explain: lo = 0, hi = 1, mid = 0. 3 < 3 is false, so the code takes the else branch as if the right half [3, 1] were sorted — and that is precisely where the drop is. The check 3 < 1 is false → hi = −1, answer −1. With <= the single-element left “half” [3] counts as sorted, 1 is not in it → lo = 1 → found.
cards/6/title: The minimum and the rotation point
cards/6/body:
Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array (LeetCode #153): the same array without duplicates, find the minimum in O(log n). The minimum sits right after the drop, and its index is how far the array was rotated.

Compare the middle with the right end. If a[mid] > a[hi], there is a drop on (mid, hi] — the minimum is to the right: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise [mid..hi] is sorted, and the minimum is not to the right of mid: hi = mid. The invariant is the minimum is in [lo..hi]; the loop is while (lo < hi), as in lower_bound.

Why not the left end: a[mid] > a[lo] holds both in [3, 4, 5, 1, 2], where the minimum is to the right, and in the unrotated [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], where the minimum is a[lo] itself. Comparing with lo cannot tell these apart, comparing with hi can: if there is no drop on (mid, hi], then a[mid] < a[hi].

That gives a second solution to #33 — in two passes: find the index k of the minimum, then run a plain search in whichever of [0..k − 1] and [k..n − 1] covers target. Also O(log n), and easier to get right.
cards/7/q: FindMin was rewritten to compare with the left end: if (a[mid] > a[lo]) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid. On which array does it return a wrong index?
cards/7/explain: The unrotated array: mid = 2, 3 > 1 → lo = 3, although the minimum is index 0, which was just thrown away. The code then returns 3. On the other two arrays it gets lucky: in [3, 4, 5, 1, 2] 5 > 3 → lo = 3, then 1 > 1 is false → hi = 3, answer 3; in [4, 5, 1, 2, 3] 1 > 4 is false → hi = 2, then 5 > 4 → lo = 2, answer 2. Both are correct.
cards/7/wrong/1: Here it gets lucky: 5 > 3 → lo = 3, then 1 > 1 is false → hi = 3. Answer 3 — correct.
cards/7/wrong/2: Correct here too: 1 > 4 is false → hi = 2, then 5 > 4 → lo = 2. Answer 2 — the index of the one.
cards/8/body:
Search in Rotated Sorted Array II (LeetCode #81): the same, but values may repeat, and you only return true or false. The key rule stops working: if a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi], you cannot tell which half is sorted. In [1, 1, 1, 2, 1] and [1, 2, 1, 1, 1] with lo = 0, hi = 4, both ends and the middle are ones, but the two sits in different halves.

What you can do: target ≠ a[mid] — that has been checked — so it is also ≠ a[lo] and ≠ a[hi], since they equal a[mid]. Both ends can go: lo++, hi--. The invariant survives, but this step discards two elements rather than half. As soon as at least one end differs from the middle, the “one half is sorted” rule works again.

The worst case is O(n), and that is not a weakness of the code but a property of the problem: in an array of ones with a single two anywhere, you cannot know whether the two is in a cell you have not looked at. Any algorithm that reads the cells of the array reads all of them in the worst case. That is the answer to the follow-up “how do duplicates affect complexity”.
cards/9/q: What is true about searching a rotated array with duplicates (#81)? Select all.
cards/9/options/0: If a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi], both ends can be discarded: they equal a[mid], and a[mid] ≠ target
cards/9/options/1: The worst case is O(n), and no algorithm can do better
cards/9/options/2: Replacing <= with < is enough to keep O(log n)
cards/9/options/3: If the input has no duplicates, this code works like the #33 solution — in O(log n)
cards/9/options/4: Sorting before the search brings the whole call back to O(log n)
cards/9/explain: The ends equal the middle, and the middle is not target, so dropping them loses nothing. The worst case is ones with a single two: any algorithm has to look into every cell. Without duplicates “all three equal” only happens when lo == mid == hi, and the code behaves like #33. A different comparison sign does not remove the ambiguity, and sorting alone is already O(n log n).
cards/10/q: You are solving Search in Rotated Sorted Array (#33) out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: are the numbers distinct? Can the array be unrotated? What to return if target is absent?
cards/10/items/1: Naive: a linear scan — O(n), while the problem asks for O(log n)
cards/10/items/2: Idea: the rotation point lands in only one half, the other one is sorted
cards/10/items/3: Code: pick the sorted half by a[lo] ≤ a[mid] and check target against its ends
cards/10/items/4: Run [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2] with target = 0: 7 → right, 1 → left, answer 4
cards/10/items/5: Complexity: O(log n) time, O(1) memory
cards/10/items/6: Edge cases: one and two elements (mid == lo), an unrotated array, duplicates
cards/10/explain: The question about duplicates at the clarification step changes everything: with them the worst case is O(n), and that is worth saying upfront. The two-element case is your cue to explain the <= in the condition.
cards/11/body:
A rotated sorted array is two sorted parts back to back, and every number of the second part is smaller than every number of the first. So any segment [lo..hi] contains at most one drop, and at least one half is free of it. With distinct numbers, a[lo] <= a[mid] is equivalent to lo and mid being in the same part — that is, no drop between them.

Minimum with duplicates (#154): if a[mid] == a[hi], the right end can be trimmed — hi--: the minimum is not lost, because the same value stays at a[mid]. The worst case is O(n) again, as in #81.

Search in a “mountain” (Find in Mountain Array, #1095): the array first rises, then falls. Find the peak with binary search, like Find Peak Element in the previous lesson, then run a plain search on each slope; on the descending one the comparison is reversed.
cards/11/deep:
One pass or two. Both are O(log n): two passes take up to 2·(⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1) iterations, one pass half as many, but with a more complex loop body. In an interview, pick the one you can talk through without mistakes: two passes reduce the problem to pieces you have already proven — FindMin and plain search.

A ring buffer with a known head. Searching the history by time is a plain binary search over the “virtual” index a[(head + k) % n]. A modulo on every step costs more than a comparison; if the capacity is a power of two, write & (n − 1). Or skip the arithmetic: the two sorted parts AsSpan(head) and AsSpan(0, head), compare target with a[0], the start of the newer part, and run MemoryExtensions.BinarySearch on the right one — with no copying.

Why #81 cannot beat O(n). An adversary argument: while the algorithm asks about cells, the adversary answers “1”. As long as at least one cell is unexamined, it may hold either 1 or 2 — both arrays are valid (they are rotations of [1, …, 1, 2]), yet the answers to “is there a 2” differ. So an algorithm that stops earlier is wrong on one of them.

Why there is no lower_bound here. A rotated array is not monotonic, so “the first element ≥ x” is not a boundary in it. What is monotonic is the predicate “the element belongs to the second part”, i.e. a[i] < a[0]: false…false, true…true. FindMin is a lower_bound over that predicate, except it compares with a[hi] so that an unrotated array works too.
cards/12/q: Match the condition with the technique.
cards/12/pairs/4/1: Plain search over index (head + k) % n
